source: Notion: H2 FY27 Maker Day themes + app ideas

apps.point: Skipped upgrades pile up as tech debt until something breaks.
apps.on_screen: A live map of a pretend dev environment. Every dependency counts down to end of support. Upgrade it and it turns green; ignore it and it fails, taking its dependents down in a chain of red alerts and pager noise.
apps.backend: None (built-in versions). Optional: paste a real package.json to check it against the npm registry.
apps.award_criterion: Best case for paying down tech debt
apps.build_prompt:
Build a Maker Day demo app called "Upgrade or Else" in the renderinc/render-on-render repo, on branch maker-day-2026/upgrade-or-else, as a single self-contained HTML file (inline CSS and JS; CDN libraries are fine). Deploy it with the repo's smallest web template and a Blueprint to the Maker Day 2026 workspace.

The point: skipped upgrades pile up as tech debt until something breaks.

Scene (1920x1080, readable from across a room): a live dependency map of a pretend dev environment. About 15 nodes (fictional packages like "tinyqueue 0.9" or "glowdb-client 4.2") connect by arrows up to three apps at the top: "Storefront", "Checkout" and "Search". Each node shows its version and a countdown ring to end of support that shifts green, then amber, then red. A calendar in the corner runs one in-game year every 10 seconds.

Controls:
- Click a node to upgrade it: a short progress bar, a big version bump (2.1 -> 3.0), and the ring resets with a green glow. Upgrading while amber takes 1 second; upgrading once red takes 4 seconds because its dependents need changes too.
- "Skip this sprint" fast-forwards 3 months.
- When a ring hits zero, the node cracks and turns red, and the failure travels down its arrows one hop at a time. Each dependent flashes a red alert with a pager buzz until an app at the top goes dark with "Outage".
- A "Debt" meter shows total months past end of support.

Key moment: run once skipping everything (cascade, outage), then reset and upgrade as rings turn amber (everything stays green, every app stays up).

Constraints: fictional package names and versions only; big type and bold animation; put colors, labels, copy and the dependency graph in one config object at the top so any theme can reskin it. Optional stretch: a "Paste package.json" box that checks versions against the public npm registry from the browser.

Done when: skipping for two in-game years always cascades into at least one app outage, steady upgrades keep every app up, and a full run takes under 90 seconds.

apps.point: Blameless postmortems teach the most, but hardly anyone reads them.
apps.on_screen: A pasted incident write-up replays as a movie: services light up on a map, alerts fire, chat messages pop in, and a scrubber rewinds to the moment it went wrong.
apps.backend: One LLM call turns the write-up into a timeline. Sample incidents included.
apps.award_criterion: Makes a hard lesson impossible to forget
apps.build_prompt:
Build a Maker Day demo app called "Postmortem Theater" in the renderinc/render-on-render repo, on branch maker-day-2026/postmortem-theater. Use the repo's smallest web service template with a Blueprint, deployed to the Maker Day 2026 workspace. Add one server endpoint, POST /api/timeline, that sends a pasted incident write-up to an LLM and returns a JSON timeline of events (timestamp, service, type: alert / chat / deploy / fix, text). The API key lives in a Render environment variable, never in the browser. Ship 3 fictional sample incidents with pre-built timelines as canned fallbacks, so the demo still works if the call fails.

The point: blameless postmortems teach the most, but hardly anyone reads them.

Scene (1920x1080, readable from across a room): the left two-thirds is a map of fictional services as boxes with connecting lines; the right third is an incident chat pane. Along the bottom runs a movie-style scrubber with play/pause and 1x/4x speed. As it plays, services glow amber then red, alerts fire as banners, chat messages pop in from roles (On-call, Incident lead, Support), and deploy markers drop onto the scrubber.

Controls: a paste box plus "Load sample" buttons; play/pause; drag the scrubber; and a red "Rewind to the moment" button. That button jumps to the triggering event, freezes the frame, spotlights the service involved, and shows a "What we learned" callout. The replay ends on a celebratory card: time to recover, the fix, and 3 improvements the team shipped.

Blameless by design: the LLM prompt must describe systems and decisions, use roles instead of names, and never assign blame.

Constraints: fictional/sample data only; big type and bold animation; put colors, labels and copy in one config object at the top so any theme can reskin it; keep the back end to this one endpoint plus static files.

Done when: each sample incident replays fully in under 60 seconds, "Rewind to the moment" lands on the root-cause event, and with the API key removed all samples still play from the fallbacks.

apps.point: Idle, oversized infrastructure quietly wastes money.
apps.on_screen: Each service is a stack of cash, and idle ones visibly burn. Sliders right-size plans and pause unused services while a savings counter climbs.
apps.backend: None. Sample data or a pasted CSV of services and plans.
apps.award_criterion: Biggest savings found, on paper
apps.build_prompt:
Build a Maker Day demo app called "Burn Rate" in the renderinc/render-on-render repo, on branch maker-day-2026/burn-rate, as a single self-contained HTML file (inline CSS and JS; CDN libraries are fine). Deploy it with the repo's smallest web template and a Blueprint to the Maker Day 2026 workspace.

The point: idle, oversized infrastructure quietly wastes money.

Scene (1920x1080, readable from across a room): a row of about 12 fictional services ("image-resizer", "nightly-report", "staging-old", "search-api") drawn as stacks of cash whose height is monthly cost. Under each stack: its plan size and a CPU/memory utilization bar. Idle services (under 10% use) have flames licking the top of the stack, with bills curling into ash and floating away. Oversized services (under 30% use on a large plan) smolder. Top right, two big counters: "Burning $X/month" in red and "Saved $Y/year" in green.

Controls:
- A plan slider on each service (XS, S, M, L, XL, with sample prices in config). Sliding down shrinks the stack, cools the flames and ticks the savings counter up with a coin sound.
- A "Pause" toggle freezes the stack in blue ice and puts the flames out.
- Sliding a busy service below what its utilization needs makes the stack wobble with a "Too small" warning, and that change does not count as savings. Right-sizing, not just cutting.
- "Right-size all" animates every fix at once.
- A "Paste CSV" box (name, plan, monthly cost, utilization) replaces the sample data.

Key moment: open on a room of burning stacks, then right-size and pause until the fire is out and the yearly savings number lands big in the center.

Constraints: fictional/sample data and prices only; big type and bold animation; put colors, labels, prices and copy in one config object at the top so any theme can reskin it; no back end.

Done when: the sample data opens with at least 3 visibly burning services, fixing them puts out every flame and shows the annual savings total, and undersizing a busy service shows a warning instead of adding savings.

apps.point: A new hire's first deploy shows how good the developer experience really is.
apps.on_screen: A timed obstacle course from laptop to live app (request access, find the docs, fix the env var, wait for review). Removing a step live cuts the timer.
apps.backend: None. Steps are configurable to mirror a real setup guide.
apps.award_criterion: Friction removed, measured in minutes
apps.build_prompt:
Build a Maker Day demo app called "First Deploy Speedrun" in the renderinc/render-on-render repo, on branch maker-day-2026/first-deploy-speedrun, as a single self-contained HTML file (inline CSS and JS; CDN libraries are fine). Deploy it with the repo's smallest web template and a Blueprint to the Maker Day 2026 workspace.

The point: a new hire's first deploy shows how good the developer experience really is.

Scene (1920x1080, readable from across a room): a side-scrolling obstacle course. A runner (a little laptop with legs) goes from a "Laptop" start line to a "Live app" finish flag. Each obstacle is a step from a setup guide, with a sample duration in minutes: "Request access" (a locked gate), "Install toolchain" (a climbing wall), "Find the docs" (a hedge maze), "Fix the env var" (a puzzle door), "Wait for review" (a toll booth), "First build" (a conveyor belt). A huge speedrun timer counts in-game minutes (compressed so a full run takes about 20 real seconds), with a split per step.

Controls:
- "Start run".
- A side panel lists each step with an improvement toggle: "Pre-granted access", "One-command setup", "Docs link in README", "Env var in template", "Review via CI checks". Toggling during a run makes that obstacle crumble or shrink, and the timer drops with a gold split.
- "Race my old time" replays a ghost runner of the previous run next to the new one.

Review is good practice, so it gets faster (automated checks), never removed. Frame every change as a win the team shipped.

Key moment: the first run finishes at a slow sample time; after 3 toggles the new runner beats its ghost by a wide margin and a "New personal best" banner fires with confetti.

Constraints: fictional/sample data only; big type and bold animation; put colors, labels, copy and the step list with durations in one config object at the top so it can mirror any real setup guide; no back end.

Done when: the default course takes at least 45 in-game minutes, each toggle visibly cuts its split, and the ghost race clearly shows the before and after in under 60 seconds.

apps.point: The farther users are from the region an app is deployed in, the slower it feels.
apps.on_screen: A 3D globe. The same tiny app is deployed to several Render regions, and everyone in the room pings each copy from their phone. Arcs fly from the venue to each region and back, labeled with the measured round-trip time: the nearby region answers almost instantly, the far ones visibly lag.
apps.backend: Light: one tiny ping service deployed to 2–3 Render regions.
apps.award_criterion: Geography as a feature
apps.build_prompt:
Build a Maker Day demo app called "Latency Globe" in the renderinc/render-on-render repo, on branch maker-day-2026/latency-globe. Use the repo's smallest web service template with a Blueprint and Render Key Value, deployed to the Maker Day 2026 workspace. The Blueprint deploys the same tiny ping service to 3 Render regions (for example Oregon, Frankfurt and Singapore), plus one main service that serves the big-screen page, the phone page and the results API.

The point: the farther users are from the region an app is deployed in, the slower it feels.

Endpoints: GET /ping on each regional copy (CORS on, returns its region name); POST /api/results and GET /api/results on the main service, backed by Key Value. Use anonymous random IDs only.

Big screen (1920x1080, readable from across a room): a slowly rotating 3D globe (globe.gl or three.js from a CDN) with a pin for the venue (lat/long in config) and a pin for each region. A QR code in the corner says "Scan to ping the world". A leaderboard on the right shows each region's median round-trip time and ping count, colored green (under 50 ms), amber, or red (over 150 ms).

Phone page (/join): one giant "Ping the world" button. Each tap pings every region 5 times from the phone's browser, times each round trip with performance.now(), and posts the medians.

The moment: as results arrive, arcs fly from the venue to each region and back. Arc travel time is the measured round trip slowed 10x so it is visible, with a ms label at the far end. When the whole room taps together, dozens of arcs snap back from the nearby region while the far ones visibly crawl.

Constraints: fictional/sample data only; big type and bold animation; put colors, labels, regions and copy in one config object at the top so any theme can reskin it; keep the back end to these few endpoints. Add a "Simulate room" button with sample latencies in case the venue Wi-Fi is weak.

Done when: a phone that scans the QR code shows its arcs on the globe within 2 seconds, the nearest region has the lowest median, and simulate mode runs the full show with no phones.

apps.point: A sales pipeline hides stalled deals in rows of a spreadsheet.
apps.on_screen: Each deal is a fish that grows as it moves through stages, drifts down as it goes quiet and falls to the bottom after 30 days stuck. Won deals leap out with a splash.
apps.backend: None. Sample deals or a pasted CRM export.
apps.award_criterion: Best at getting stale work noticed
apps.build_prompt:
Build a Maker Day demo app called "Pipeline Aquarium" in the renderinc/render-on-render repo, on branch maker-day-2026/pipeline-aquarium, as a single self-contained HTML file (inline CSS and JS; CDN libraries are fine). Deploy it with the repo's smallest web template and a Blueprint to the Maker Day 2026 workspace.

The point: a sales pipeline hides stalled deals in rows of a spreadsheet.

Scene (1920x1080, readable from across a room): a wide aquarium split left to right by strands of kelp into stages: Lead, Qualified, Demo, Proposal, Negotiation. Each deal is a fish sized by deal value and labeled with a fictional company ("Blue Heron Bakery", "Copperline Freight"). Fish grow a size as they move to the next stage. Height in the water shows activity: recently touched deals swim near the surface; a deal that goes quiet slowly drifts down; after 30 days stuck in one stage it sinks to the sand, turns grey and its bubbles stop.

Controls:
- "Play week by week" advances time so drift and growth animate.
- Click a fish to "Follow up": it perks up, blows bubbles and rises to the surface.
- Drag a fish right to advance its stage.
- When a deal is won, the fish leaps out of the water on the far right with a big splash and lands in a "Won" trophy bowl, with a cheer.
- A "Spreadsheet view" toggle shows the exact same deals as a plain table, where stalled rows look like every other row.
- A "Paste CSV" box (name, value, stage, last activity date) replaces the sample deals.

Key moment: start in the spreadsheet view and ask the room which deals are stuck. Flip to the aquarium: the sunken fish on the sand answer it instantly. Follow up on them and watch the tank come alive.

Constraints: fictional/sample data only; big type and bold animation; put colors, labels, stages and copy in one config object at the top so any theme can reskin it; no back end.

Done when: the sample data has at least 4 sunken fish that are not obvious in the table view, a follow-up lifts a fish back up, and a won deal triggers the leap and splash.

apps.point: Support teams answer the same question again and again instead of fixing why people ask.
apps.on_screen: Tickets fall like Tetris blocks, colored by topic. Answering one clears one block; writing a help article clears every block of that color.
apps.backend: None. Optional LLM call groups real pasted tickets by topic.
apps.award_criterion: Fix the source, not the symptom
apps.build_prompt:
Build a Maker Day demo app called "Ticket Tetris" in the renderinc/render-on-render repo, on branch maker-day-2026/ticket-tetris, as a single self-contained HTML file (inline CSS and JS; CDN libraries are fine). Deploy it with the repo's smallest web template and a Blueprint to the Maker Day 2026 workspace.

The point: support teams answer the same question again and again instead of fixing why people ask.

Scene (1920x1080, readable from across a room): a tall Tetris well in the center. Tickets fall as blocks colored by topic, each showing a short fictional subject line: "Password reset" (blue), "Custom domain setup" (purple), "Billing question" (yellow), "Build failed" (orange). Blocks arrive faster over time and stack up. A legend on the left lists each topic with a live count; a scoreboard on the right shows Answered, Deflected and Articles published.

Controls:
- Click a block to "Answer" it: it pops and clears, +1 Answered.
- Each topic in the legend has a "Write help article" button. Writing takes 5 seconds (a progress bar with a typing sound). When it publishes, every block of that color clears at once in a big cascade, and new tickets of that topic arrive at a third of the rate. Deflected tickets fly off to a "Solved by docs" tray.
- "Restart" resets the well.

Key moment: for the first 30 seconds, answer one block at a time and the stack still climbs. Then write two articles, and the well empties and stays calm. End on a summary card: "Every article is a question nobody has to ask again," with answered vs deflected totals.

Celebrate the support team: answering is good work, and the articles multiply it.

Constraints: fictional/sample data only; big type and bold animation; put colors, labels, topics, arrival rates and copy in one config object at the top so any theme can reskin it; no back end (leave out the optional LLM grouping; topics come from the sample data).

Done when: answering alone can't keep up with the sample arrival rate, an article clears every block of its color and lowers that topic's arrival rate, and a full game with the before/after summary runs in under 90 seconds.

apps.point: Recognition stays inside teams, which hides silos.
apps.on_screen: A night sky where each person is a star. Kudos sent from phones draw lines of light; cross-team lines glow brightest, revealing who connects the company and which groups are islands.
apps.backend: Light: a small web service stores kudos; the big screen polls it.
apps.award_criterion: Best at making connections visible
apps.build_prompt:
Build a Maker Day demo app called "Kudos Constellation" in the renderinc/render-on-render repo, on branch maker-day-2026/kudos-constellation. Use the repo's smallest web service template with a Blueprint and a small Postgres (one kudos table: from, to, message, created_at), deployed to the Maker Day 2026 workspace. It has a big-screen page and a phone page the room joins with a QR code.

The point: recognition stays inside teams, which hides silos.

Endpoints: GET /api/people (the fictional roster from config), POST /api/kudos, GET /api/kudos?since=<id>. The big screen polls every second.

Big screen (1920x1080, readable from across a room): a night sky with about 40 stars, each a fictional person, grouped by fictional team (Platform, Support, Sales, Design, Finance, People) into constellations with soft team labels. Seed it with sample kudos that mostly stay within teams, so the sky opens as bright islands. A QR code in the corner says "Scan to send some light." A side panel shows "Bridges built" (cross-team kudos), the top bridge builders, and any team with no cross-team lines yet, gently dimmed with a prompt like "Send some light to Finance."

Phone page (/join): pick a star to play as, pick a star to thank, type a short message (80 characters max), tap Send.

The moment: each kudos fires a shooting star from sender to receiver, leaving a line of light. Same-team lines are thin and soft; cross-team lines glow bright gold and pulse. Stars grow brighter as they gain connections. As the room plays, the islands join up into one connected web.

Constraints: fictional/sample data only; big type and bold animation; put colors, labels, roster and copy in one config object at the top so any theme can reskin it; keep the back end to these few endpoints. Add a simple word blocklist, a length limit, and an admin "Reset sky" button.

Done when: a phone kudos appears on the big screen within 2 seconds, cross-team lines are clearly brighter than same-team lines, and the islands panel empties once every team has a cross-team connection.

apps.point: Planning isn't just splitting a fixed pie: some investments make everything around them grow.
apps.on_screen: The budget is a city, each team a district. Players place their funding, then fast-forward a year: each district grows by its projected return, and shared investments like roads and power lines lift every district they connect. Everyone's city goes up side by side to compare strategies.
apps.backend: None. Sample numbers, not real budgets.
apps.award_criterion: Best at showing how smart investments grow the whole pie
apps.build_prompt:
Build a Maker Day demo app called "Budget City" in the renderinc/render-on-render repo, on branch maker-day-2026/budget-city, as a single self-contained HTML file (inline CSS and JS; CDN libraries are fine). Deploy it with the repo's smallest web template and a Blueprint to the Maker Day 2026 workspace.

The point: planning isn't just splitting a fixed pie: some investments make everything around them grow.

Scene (1920x1080, readable from across a room): an isometric city map with 5 districts, each a fictional team (Engineering, Sales, Support, Marketing, People) drawn as a cluster of small buildings. Each district shows its projected yearly return (sample values, for example 4-12%). Between districts are empty lots for shared investments: roads, power lines and a transit line. Each shared investment has a cost and a boost that applies to every district it connects.

Controls:
- 2-4 players take turns on the same screen. Each gets 100 sample coins.
- Click + / - on a district to fund it, or click a lot to build a shared investment (a road draws itself between districts; power lines spark).
- "Fast-forward a year": a 12-month animation where buildings rise floor by floor at each district's return, and connected districts glow and grow extra floors as boosts kick in.
- After every player finishes, "Compare cities" places all cities side by side with their final value and a callout: "Shared investments added +X".

Key moment: one player piles everything into the highest-return district; another spreads funding and builds a road and a power line. On the compare screen, the connected city is visibly taller and worth more.

Tune the sample numbers so a balanced plan with shared investments reliably beats the all-in plan, but not by a silly margin.

Constraints: fictional/sample numbers only, not real budgets; big type and bold animation; put colors, labels, districts, returns, boosts and copy in one config object at the top so any theme can reskin it; no back end.

Done when: the all-in strategy loses to a balanced plan with shared investments using the default numbers, the year animation shows boosted districts growing faster, and a 2-player round runs in under 3 minutes.

apps.point: A message loses its meaning as it passes through layers of an organization.
apps.on_screen: An announcement travels a relay of people cards (exec, manager, lead, team, all-hands). At each stop an LLM retells it; changed words turn red, and the final version sits next to the original.
apps.award_criterion: Say it clearly the first time
apps.build_prompt:
Build a Maker Day demo app called "Game of Telephone" in the renderinc/render-on-render repo, on branch maker-day-2026/game-of-telephone. Use the repo's smallest web service template with a Blueprint, deployed to the Maker Day 2026 workspace. Add one server endpoint, POST /api/retell { text, stop }, that calls an LLM with a short persona prompt for that stop and returns the retold message. The API key lives in a Render environment variable, never in the browser. Include canned retellings for every stop of the sample announcements, so the demo still works if the call fails.

The point: a message loses its meaning as it passes through layers of an organization.

Scene (1920x1080, readable from across a room): five people cards in a horizontal relay: Exec, Manager, Lead, Team, All-hands. They are fictional roles with friendly illustrated avatars, not real people. Each persona retells in good faith: the Exec condenses to strategy, the Manager adds priorities, the Lead turns it into tasks, the Team retells it as a casual chat message, All-hands boils it to one headline.

Controls: a text box for the announcement, "Load sample" buttons (one vague, one clear), and "Send it down the line". A glowing envelope travels card to card. At each stop the retelling types out under the card, with a word-level diff against the previous version (jsdiff from a CDN): changed words in red, dropped words struck through. A "Meaning kept" meter drops from 100% using a simple overlap score.

Key moment: the final version appears big, side by side with the original. Then press "Say it clearly": run the clear sample (short, one date, one action). It survives the relay with the meter still high, and a banner reads "Said clearly the first time."

Constraints: fictional/sample data only; big type and bold animation; put colors, labels, personas and copy in one config object at the top so any theme can reskin it; keep the back end to this one endpoint plus static files.

Done when: the vague sample ends with visibly changed meaning and a low meter, the clear sample keeps its key facts through all five stops, and with the API key removed both samples still play from canned responses.

apps.point: People notice a change in sound faster than a change on a dashboard.
apps.on_screen: Every service is an instrument in one ambient song. Errors play off-key, rising latency slows the tempo, and a quiet service drops out of the mix, with a visualizer pulsing along.
apps.backend: None (simulated metrics). Optional: poll a real metrics endpoint.
apps.award_criterion: Heard the problem before anyone got paged
apps.build_prompt:
Build a Maker Day demo app called "Service Soundscape" in the renderinc/render-on-render repo, on branch maker-day-2026/service-soundscape, as a single self-contained HTML file (inline CSS and JS; CDN libraries are fine). Deploy it with the repo's smallest web template and a Blueprint to the Maker Day 2026 workspace.

The point: people notice a change in sound faster than a change on a dashboard.

Scene (1920x1080, readable from across a room): a pulsing radial visualizer in the center, with one ring per instrument. Around it sit 6 tiles for fictional services, each with a live sparkline and its instrument: api-gateway (bass), database (warm pads), queue-worker (hi-hat), auth (bell arpeggio), search (marimba), cache (shaker). Together they play one calm ambient loop in a major key (Tone.js from a CDN). Simulated metrics tick every second.

Mapping:
- Error rate rising: that instrument's notes bend off-key, and its tile shakes red.
- Latency rising: the tempo slows for the whole song.
- Traffic dropping to zero: the instrument fades out of the mix and its tile goes silent grey.

Controls: a big "Start the music" button (browsers need a click for audio). A presenter panel, toggled with H, has fault buttons: "Error spike on auth", "Slow database", "Queue worker stops", "Heal all". A "Blindfold" toggle blurs the tiles, so the room has only the sound.

Key moment: turn on Blindfold, press a fault without saying which, and ask the room to name the service. Keep the fault small enough that the dashboard numbers barely move but the sound clearly changes. Then reveal and "Heal all", and the song resolves back into harmony.

Constraints: fictional/sample data only; big type and bold animation; put colors, labels, services, instruments and copy in one config object at the top so any theme can reskin it; no back end. Optional stretch: a config URL that polls a real metrics endpoint.

Done when: each fault is clearly audible within 3 seconds, "Heal all" returns the song to its calm loop, and the audience can pick the right service in Blindfold mode.

apps.point: Request logs hold patterns nobody looks at.
apps.on_screen: Drop in a sample log and get a horoscope-style profile of your traffic: peak hours are its sleep schedule, top referrers its best friends, one-time visitors its fleeting romances, anomalies its secrets. Charts sit alongside.
apps.backend: None (the log is parsed in the browser). Optional LLM call writes the prose.
apps.award_criterion: Best insight found in plain sight
apps.build_prompt:
Build a Maker Day demo app called "Traffic Horoscope" in the renderinc/render-on-render repo, on branch maker-day-2026/traffic-horoscope, as a single self-contained HTML file (inline CSS and JS; CDN libraries are fine). Deploy it with the repo's smallest web template and a Blueprint to the Maker Day 2026 workspace.

The point: request logs hold patterns nobody looks at.

Scene (1920x1080, readable from across a room): a starry backdrop with a big drop zone, "Drop your log here", and a "Use sample log" button. Generate the sample in the browser: about 5,000 lines of fictional traffic in Common Log Format for "moonbeam-bakery.example", with planted patterns (a lunchtime peak and a 9 pm peak, one dominant referrer, many one-time visitors, a burst from one IP at 3 am, a 404 path that gets hit often). Also accept JSON-lines logs. Parse in a Web Worker; the file never leaves the browser.

The reveal: the stars swirl, then a zodiac-style card flips over with a sign derived from the peak hour ("Your traffic is a Night Owl, rising sign: Lunch Rush"). Five sections appear one at a time, each with a chart beside it and the real number that justifies it:
- Sleep schedule: quietest and busiest hours, on a 24-hour radial clock.
- Best friends: top referrers, as a bar chart.
- Fleeting romances: share of one-time visitors, as a donut.
- Secrets: anomalies (bursts, 404 hotspots, odd user agents), on a sparkline with the spike circled.
- Forecast: a playful one-liner based on the traffic trend.

Write the prose from templates filled with the computed numbers (leave out the optional LLM). Keep the tone warm and funny.

Constraints: fictional/sample data only; big type and bold animation; put colors, labels, sign names and copy templates in one config object at the top so any theme can reskin it; no back end.

Done when: the sample log produces all five sections, each citing a real number from the log; the planted 3 am burst shows up under Secrets; and a 50,000-line log parses and reveals in under 3 seconds.

apps.point: Noisy alerts wear people out and train them to ignore the real ones.
apps.on_screen: A 3am survival game. Alerts arrive while a sleep meter drains; triage them before your energy runs out, or fix a noisy alert for good so it stops coming back. Surviving until morning wins.
apps.award_criterion: Best case for alert hygiene
apps.build_prompt:
Build a Maker Day demo app called "On-Call Survival" in the renderinc/render-on-render repo, on branch maker-day-2026/on-call-survival, as a single self-contained HTML file (inline CSS and JS; CDN libraries are fine). Deploy it with the repo's smallest web template and a Blueprint to the Maker Day 2026 workspace.

The point: noisy alerts wear people out and train them to ignore the real ones.

Scene (1920x1080, readable from across a room): a dark bedroom at 3:00am. A big clock ticks from 3:00 to 7:00 (one game hour = 15 seconds). A "Sleep" meter across the top drains a little every time an alert card lands. Alert cards drop onto a phone on the nightstand: most are noisy repeats ("disk 71% on fake-worker-3", "CPU blip on sample-api"), a few are real and marked only by subtle detail ("checkout error rate 18%").

Controls:
- "Ack" on a card: clears it but costs sleep; noisy alerts return a few seconds later.
- "Fix for good" on a noisy card: costs more sleep once, then that alert type is struck off a "Noise sources" list and never returns.
- A real alert that sits unhandled for 10 seconds turns red and costs a big chunk of sleep.
Key moment: by 5am a player who only acks is buried in a flood of repeats and misses the real alert; a player who fixed the noisy ones sees the phone go quiet, spots the real alert at once, and the sun rises with a "Slept through the night" banner.

Endpoints (keep it to these): GET / (big screen), GET /play (phone page), POST /shot (does ~30 ms of light work and returns its RENDER_INSTANCE_ID), GET /stats (counts for the big screen to poll). Each response is a ball arcing in from the crowd (sampled so it stays smooth): a save if it returns 2xx within 1 second, a goal on an error or timeout. Keepers are the distinct instance ids seen in the last 10 seconds, each labeled with a short id; a new one dives in when a new instance answers. Scene (1920x1080, readable from across a room): a cutaway house at night with bright rooms and six appliances (lamp, fridge, TV, kettle, fan, toaster), each a dependency the app calls. Glowing dots flow along wires from a fuse box to each appliance (calls). The house shares one power budget, shown as a big "House brightness" meter.

Controls:
- "Faulty toaster" toggle: the toaster starts sparking and every call to it hangs for a few seconds before failing. Waiting calls pile up on its wire and draw power, so without a breaker the whole house dims room by room and the other appliances slow down.
- "Install breaker" toggle for the toaster's circuit, with a visible breaker switch in the fuse box. Done when: without a breaker, the faulty toaster dims the whole house below 50% brightness; with a breaker, it trips within a few seconds and brightness recovers above 90%; after "Fix toaster", the next test call resets the breaker to CLOSED.

The point: A brand sounds strongest when every channel sings the same song.

apps.point: Building for other languages and regions early makes a product feel local everywhere.
apps.on_screen: A fictional restaurant menu opens in five cities. Hard-coded text overflows its boxes in longer languages, prices show the wrong currency and dates read backwards. Players pull the text out for translation and fix the formats, and diners around the world order happily.
apps.award_criterion: Best at showing why localization matters
apps.build_prompt:

The point: building for other languages and regions early makes a product feel local everywhere.

Scene (1920x1080, readable from across a room): a fictional restaurant, "Bistro Nimbus", opens in five cities at once. Five menu cards sit side by side (for example Berlin, Tokyo, Cairo, Paris and Sao Paulo), each with a small queue of diner avatars in front of it.

Before: the menu was built with hard-coded English text in fixed-size boxes. Long German dish names overflow and get clipped, the Arabic card reads left-to-right, every price shows "$" and the "Opening night" date is ambiguous (03/04 or 04/03?). Diners show puzzled thought bubbles and a "Confused diners" counter ticks up.

Controls: three big fix buttons, usable in any order:
- "Extract strings" - the text lifts out of every card into a glowing translation tray, comes back translated from a sample dictionary, boxes resize to fit and the Arabic card mirrors to right-to-left.
- "Localize prices" - prices spin like coins and land in the right currency and format via Intl.NumberFormat.
- "Localize dates" - dates flip like a desk calendar into each locale's format via Intl.DateTimeFormat.

apps.point: The best deals come from finding what each side values most.
apps.on_screen: Two players at a market stall negotiate over several things at once: price, delivery date and extras. Each has hidden priorities. Trading on single items stalls, but discovering what the other side cares about grows a shared "value pie" on screen until both walk away happy.
apps.award_criterion: Best at showing win-win negotiation
apps.build_prompt:
Build a Maker Day demo app called "Market Day" in the renderinc/render-on-render repo, on branch maker-day-2026/market-day, as a single self-contained HTML file (inline CSS and JS; CDN libraries are fine). Deploy it with the repo's smallest web template and a Blueprint to the Maker Day 2026 workspace.

The point: the best deals come from finding what each side values most.

Scene (1920x1080, readable from across a room): a sunny market stall. On the left, the seller, "Juniper's Jam Stall"; on the right, the buyer, "Cafe Pebble" (both fictional). Two volunteers each control one side. Between them are three big deal dials: Price, Delivery date and Extras (for example free samples or recipe cards). Above the stall is the "value pie": a circle whose size is the two sides' satisfaction added together, split into two colored slices.

Hidden priorities: at the start of each round, each side gets a face-down priority card with random weights from the config (for example the seller cares most about a later delivery date, the buyer cares most about extras).

Round 1, "Haggle on price": only the Price dial is unlocked. Each move helps one side and costs the other the same amount, so the pie never grows and only the slices shift. After a few moves a "Stalled" banner appears.

Round 2, "Find what matters": each side can press "Ask what matters" to flip one of the other side's priority cards. All three dials unlock. Trading something cheap for you but valuable to the other side makes the pie swell with a satisfying pop, and both slices grow. When both sides pass the "happy" line, they shake hands, confetti falls and a "Deal!" card shows how much bigger the pie got.

Constraints: fictional businesses and sample numbers only; big type and bold animation; put colors, labels, copy, items and weight ranges in one config object at the top so any theme can reskin it; no back end.

Done when: price-only trading never grows the pie, revealing priorities and trading across dials grows it by at least 50% with both sides happy, and a full two-round demo runs in under 90 seconds.
